## Current use

It is worth noting that total electricity use at the brewery currently stands at 3220 MWh per year, a figure that provides the essential backdrop for everything that follows in this assessment. Refrigeration accounts for the largest share of this consumption, underscoring its central importance to the site's overall energy profile, and it is examined in greater detail in the dedicated section below. The remaining electricity is consumed by a wide range of activities across the brewhouse, the cellar, packaging, and site services. Pumps are utilised to move wort, water, and beer between vessels, while motors drive mills, conveyors, and packaging machinery. Compressed air supports valves and packaging equipment, and lighting and ventilation operate across all production areas. It should be emphasised that none of these uses is metered separately in the material available to the assessment, which means that the precise split of the remaining consumption between them cannot be stated with confidence. The annual figure is a metered total for the site as a whole, and it serves as the baseline against which every potential saving discussed in this document is measured. Production volumes naturally fluctuate over the course of the year, and electricity use fluctuates alongside them; the annual total already captures this variation, since it aggregates a full twelve months of operation. Consequently, any saving expressed as a proportion of electricity use is a proportion of the metered annual total, rather than of a peak month or a design load. Specific electricity use per unit of production is not reported, as production figures were outside the material supplied. Comparisons with other breweries are likewise not attempted, for the simple reason that a meaningful comparison would require a shared basis, and no such shared basis is currently available. In essence, the current-use picture consists of a total and a ranking of uses, and it is this ranking that shapes the direction of the remainder of the assessment.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration represents the largest single use of electricity at the brewery, playing a pivotal role in the site's energy story. The fermentation process generates heat that must be continuously removed in order to maintain the temperature of the fermenting wort, and finished beer is held cold in storage until the point of dispatch. Cooling therefore operates in every month of the year, not merely during warmer weather, which means the refrigeration plant is best characterised as a continuous load rather than an intermittent one. The plant removes heat at evaporators located in the fermenters, the cold stores, and the cellar, and rejects that heat at the condensers. Compressors raise the refrigerant to the pressure at which it condenses, and it is the compressor motors that account for the majority of the electricity consumed by the plant, with condenser fans and coolant pumps accounting for the remainder. The physical condition of the plant has a direct bearing on the load. Fouled condenser surfaces push the condensing temperature upwards, forcing the compressors to work against a higher pressure for the same duty, while low refrigerant charge and worn compressor valves produce a similar effect through extended running hours. Regular cleaning of the condensers, together with the prompt repair of leaks, is therefore an important part of holding the present load at its current level, before any retrofit is even considered. At present, the heat rejected at the condensers is simply discharged into the surrounding air. This rejected heat is precisely the stream that the proposed retrofit seeks to recover: it is available whenever the plant is running, and the plant runs throughout the year. The load does, of course, vary across the seasons: higher summer ambient temperatures raise the condensing pressure and the associated compressor work, whereas winter operation lowers both. The annual electricity total already reflects this seasonal movement, and no separate monthly breakdown of the refrigeration load is available at this time.

## Steam

Steam plays a crucial role in the brewhouse, where it is responsible for heating the mash, boiling the wort, and supplying hot water for cleaning purposes. Steam is raised in the site boiler and distributed to the brewhouse through insulated mains. Condensate is returned wherever the layout permits, and returned condensate reduces the amount of fuel the boiler must burn for a given steam output. It is important to appreciate that losses from leaking traps and uninsulated fittings show up in the steam figures just as surely as genuine process use does, and a single month's record has no way of separating the two. The steam figures used in this assessment are drawn from one winter month. That month is the only steam record available, and it should not be interpreted as an annual figure. Steam demand at a brewery is inherently seasonal in nature. Space heating adds to the process load during the winter, cold feed water increases the heat required for every hot liquor preparation, and production schedules themselves vary over the course of the year. A winter month therefore tends to show steam use at or near its highest level, and simply scaling the month's figures up to form an annual total would overstate steam use for the year as a whole. For this reason, the assessment deliberately does not annualise the steam figures. They are used for two purposes only: to indicate the size of the steam load relative to the site's energy use in the month recorded, and to identify where steam is consumed within the brewhouse. Any saving that depends on steam quantities is presented subject to the same limitation. A full year of steam metering, or monthly records spanning a year, would ultimately replace the single month and remove this limitation; until such records exist, however, conclusions regarding steam necessarily remain at the level of the one month that was measured.

## Recommendation

It is recommended that the brewery should approve the heat-recovery retrofit. The retrofit is projected to deliver a saving of 18% of electricity use, which translates into a derived saving of 580 MWh per year when set against the metered total. The capital cost associated with the retrofit is $775k. At a price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out at $69552. Comparing the derived annual saving of $69552 with the capital cost of $775k gives a derived simple payback of 11.1 years. A payback of 11.1 years is admittedly long for a single measure, and the case for the retrofit ultimately rests on the sheer size and continuity of the refrigeration load: the recovered heat is available in every month of the year, because the refrigeration plant itself runs in every month. It should be noted that the payback figure is a simple payback. It takes no account of maintenance costs, of possible changes in the electricity price, or of the time value of money, and it should therefore be read as a screening figure rather than as a full investment appraisal. The recommendation set out here covers the retrofit only. The steam figures underpinning the assessment are drawn from one winter month and are accordingly flagged as seasonal. No steam measure is recommended on the basis of a single month, and gathering a full year of steam records is the logical next step before any steam saving can be properly costed. Electricity metering by individual use is likewise absent, and installing submeters on the refrigeration plant would allow the saving to be verified after installation rather than merely inferred from the site total. Subject to that reading, the retrofit stands as the one measure that the present evidence genuinely supports.
